The five grids used in the analysis were labeled A through E, with grids A-C having a matching condition along the cut line and grids D-E not having this constraint.
Grid A was generated using the GRAPE code, while grids B-E were generated using a two-step process with an embedded viscous grid.
The variation in blade surface heat transfer predictions among the five grids was small for both the finite difference and finite volume flow analysis codes.
The heat transfer predictions were sensitive to the transition modeling assumptions, especially for the high Reynolds number, high turbulence intensity case.
Using Mayle's transition model with an adjustment for local freestream turbulence intensity provided the best agreement with experimental heat transfer data.

The pitchwise variation in total pressure showed more significant differences between the grids, with the finite volume flow solver predicting a lower minimum total pressure and narrower wake compared to the finite difference solver.
Grid E, with the curved downstream periodic boundary, provided the best agreement with the experimental pitchwise total pressure data.
Increasing the grid orthogonality to the blade surface by using a larger grid did not result in significantly different heat transfer predictions.
The overall loss coefficients calculated using the two flow solvers were reasonably close to the experimental value, with the best agreement coming from grid D.
The use of the Chien two-equation turbulence model increased the predicted loss compared to the Baldwin-Lomax model.
The narrowing and deepening of the wake prediction for grid E was likely due to numerical diffusion from the coarser grid on the suction side of the cut line.
The grid generated by embedding a viscous grid within an inviscid grid (grid B) provided the best overall performance in terms of heat transfer and aerodynamic predictions.
The authors recommended the use of C-type grids generated by embedding a viscous grid within an inviscid grid for turbine heat transfer and performance analyses.
The goal of the study was to determine the effects of different C-type grid geometries on turbine blade heat transfer and aerodynamic performance.
The study used two flow analysis codes, a finite difference and a finite volume code, to compare the results for the five different grids.
